content.content:
fix: pair frame/call against a loop-only pass

frame_call_ns was a difference of two passes measuring different
code: a window mean from measure_window, minus a slope fitted at
the dither call site. The same source loop compiles differently
at the two sites — 12% apart at opt-level=0 — so the difference
landed in the result at full size, clamping frame/call to
0.000 ns in debug and biasing it ~30% low in release. Pairing
the window pass with a loop-only pass over one shared loop
cancels the loop term exactly instead of estimating it.

- src/overhead.rs
  - add #[inline(never)] run_inner, the single compiled loop
    driving all three calibration passes
  - add measure_loop_only beside measure_window; frame_call is
    now w_low - l_low
  - keep the slope-based derivation as a debug cross-check, and
    warn before clamping either frame_call or frame_sample
  - record cal_l_low_ns; refresh module and field docs
- src/main.rs: print l_low in the calibrate diagnostic block and
  in the -v raw line
- Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock: 0.22.0-1
- TODO.md: open the cycle — problem statement covering both
  constants, three-rung ladder, -1 marked done
- notes/chores/chores-04.md: open the section under the close-out
  title; -1 narrative, the call-site codegen finding, the
  one-sided contamination analysis for -2, and a -1 outcome note

content.content:
fix: fit frame/sample from a low sample quantile

The two-point fit read mean-below-p99 at both points, trimming
1% off the top. Scheduler interference is one-sided and
duration-proportional, so far more than 1% of the ~85 us N_HIGH
samples are dirty under load: the slope rotates up and the
intercept goes negative (-416.7 ns measured with a spinner on
the calibration core). A low sample quantile reads the
uncontaminated tail instead, and the four candidate discard
fractions agreed on the slope to six figures under that same
contention.

- src/overhead.rs
  - add DITHER_LOW_Q discard fractions and DitherPoint::low_q_ns;
    the production fit takes the smallest sample remaining after
    discarding the fastest 1%, at both points
  - DITHER_WINDOWS 20 -> 40 with per-window counts halved, so the
    total sample budget is unchanged
  - keep the fastest-windows mean as the fast diagnostic: window
    tail selection does not survive a continuous competitor
  - add fit_candidates(), one labelled list behind both the -v
    log and the calibrate command's stdout block
- src/main.rs
  - use fit_candidates() for the alternative-fit block; derive
    the production-fit label from the constants
  - reword the Calibration block to unit-then-role, parallel
    across all three: drop "dithered" (stale now the estimator is
    a quantile, and it described both constants equally), and say
    that frame/call is not subtracted
- Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock: 0.22.0-2
- TODO.md: -2 rung retitled to the landed approach, marked done
- notes/chores/chores-04.md: -2 narrative and outcome; withdraw
  the -1 claim that frame/call sheds contamination by
  min-over-windows

content.content:
fix: derive frame/sample without extrapolating

frame_sample_ns was the two-point fit's intercept, and a low
sample quantile parks both fit points on the clock-lattice
floor. That shared ~1-quantum bias cancels in the slope but
lands undiluted in the intercept: on the quiet r5-7600x it read
-1.2828 ns on three consecutive runs, against a paired 8.23 ns
that reproduces the "8.2 +/- 0.06 ns" this module has documented
for that box since the original estimator. So the intercept now
comes from a difference of two same-N_LOW measurements, and the
slope keeps the quantile.

- src/overhead.rs
  - frame_sample = d_low.min_window_ns - l_low, both amortized
    per-sample costs over the same run_inner; DitherPoint gains
    min_window_ns
  - add three physical checks (frame_call > 0, frame_sample >= 0,
    frame_sample <= frame_call) collected into
    Overhead::violations; the last needs no model at all, a part
    cannot exceed its whole

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**fix: calibration robust to codegen and noise**

Two calibration constants are derived by differencing or
extrapolating measurements that don't share their assumptions.
`frame_call_ns` subtracts a slope fitted at the dither call site
from a window mean measured at another — the same source loop
compiles ~12% apart at `opt-level=0`, driving `frame/call` to a
clamped `0.000 ns` in debug and ~30% low in release.
`frame_sample_ns` extrapolates a two-point fit back to N=0, and
scheduler interference is one-sided and duration-proportional,
so it inflates the long point ~100x harder than the short one,
tilting the slope up and levering the intercept negative.
Neither averages away with more runs.

- [[N]] 0.22.0-1 fix: pair frame/call against a loop-only pass
  (done)
  - shared `#[inline(never)] run_inner` across all three passes
  - `measure_loop_only` beside `measure_window`; `frame_call =
    w_low - l_low`, loop term cancelling exactly
  - warn instead of silently clamping, both constants
- [[N]] 0.22.0-2 fix: fit frame/sample from a low sample quantile
  (done)
  - discard the fastest 1% of samples, take the minimum of the
    remainder, at both fit points: the low tail is the
    uncontaminated part, and discarding its very bottom sheds
    samples that rounded down on the clock lattice
  - window-mean tail selection was tried first and failed —
    under a continuous competitor no `N_HIGH` window escapes
    contamination; kept as the `fast` diagnostic
  - `frame_sample` and `loop_per_iter` both move
- [[N]] 0.22.0-3 fix: derive frame/sample without extrapolating
  (done)
  - `frame_sample = d_low - l_low`, both at `N_LOW` over the
    same `run_inner`: a difference of same-N measurements can't
    be levered negative by a contaminated long point, because
    there is no long point in it
  - assert the physical invariant `frame_sample <= frame_call`
    (a part cannot exceed the whole) and warn when violated —
    seen at 51.323 vs 49.766 ns, an impossibility nothing
    currently checks
  - on a non-physical constant, retry a bounded number of times
    and then report it unavailable; never publish a clamp
- [[N]] 0.22.0-4 fix: report only what is applied to results
  - demote `frame/call` to `-v` and the `calibrate` command: its
    sole consumer is `pick_inner`
    (`inner = ceil(10 * frame_call / step)`), and the consequence
    (`inner`, `adj/call`) is already in the bench header
  - relabel in plain language; the current block says "per
    sample" for both framing constants without conveying that
    one is a *part of* the other
  - state what the selected benches actually subtract — the
    TProbe path (`tp-pc`, `tp2-pc`) subtracts nothing, yet the
    block advertises two subtractions
  - ordering matters: -3's invariant check is what makes hiding
    `frame/call` safe, rather than trading a visible wrong
    number for an invisible one
- [[N]] 0.22.0 close-out

**Resume here.** -1/-2/-3 are landed; -4 and close-out remain.

- -4 is specified in its rung above. -3's invariant check is
  the prerequisite: without it, demoting `frame/call` to `-v`
  trades a visible wrong number for an invisible one.
- Close-out also owes: the `--first-parent` recommendation
  alongside the
  [Merge non-ff recipe](notes/cycle-protocol.md#merge-non-ff-recipe)
  (and eventually upstream to `vc-template-x1`), the `Commits:`
  backfill for -1 and -2, and retiring older `## Done` entries.
- Publishing shape is **Merge non-ff** (trapezoid), chosen so
  the internal steps stay visible and `--first-parent` skips
  them. The merge must be set up *before* the close-out push,
  and `vc-x1 push` only fully supports keep-separate, so
  expect manual jj steps.
- Then fast-forward `main` to `fix-calibration` and rebase
  `web-claude-tweaks` onto it — that rewrites an already
  published bookmark (needs approval), and its arbitrary
  `0.21.0-b` version needs replacing.
- **r5-7600x is reachable**: plain `ssh r5-7600x` works, but
  `scp` fails with "Network is unreachable" — stream instead,
  `ssh r5-7600x 'cat > /tmp/iiac-rel && chmod +x /tmp/iiac-rel'
  < target/release/iiac-perf`. No `target-cpu=native` anywhere,
  so one release build is valid on both boxes. The copies on
  that machine predate -3.
- **Measurement gotcha**: the bot's sandbox uses `--unshare-pid`,
  so a background spinner started in one shell is invisible to
  every other one — `pgrep`/`pkill` silently find nothing and
  cannot stop it. The only reliable "machine is quiet again"
  signal is the `timeout` expiring. Two rounds of measurements
  were taken under contention before this was understood.
- **Two loose threads, neither chased**: `d_low.min_window_ns`
  swung ~8% between attempts in a quiet debug run (the
  invariant catches the fallout, but the input is unstable),
  and debug `frame_call` on r5-7600x read 11.79 / 14.72 ns
  against release's 25.4 — backwards, since an unoptimized
  timer pair should cost *more*, not less.

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber.
The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its

content.text:
I've re-read the branch, the resume notes, the web-claude-tweaks diff, and both band-table implementations. Here's my assessment.

## TL;DR

The fix-calibration branch is sound work worth resuming, not abandoning — the design is right and the resume notes are excellent. The pasted outputs are from **main** (0.21.0), so they demonstrate the exact bugs the branch already fixes, not a failure of the branch. The "bucket" oddities are mostly a known display artifact of coarse debug-build clock quanta, plus real-but-small bugs that web-claude-tweaks patches in the *other* band-table copy. My recommendation: resume the branch, chase one concrete lead I spotted on the `min_window_ns` instability, then finish -4 and close out.

## What your two runs actually show

Both runs are main's code, so:

- **Release `frame/call 47.292 ns`** — per the branch's own analysis this is ~30% low (the slope-subtraction bias); the branch measures ~higher via the paired loop-only pass.
- **Debug `frame/call 0.000 ns`** — exactly the -1 commit's diagnosis: main subtracts a slope fitted at the dither call site from a window mean at another call site, and at opt-level=0 the same source loop compiles ~12% apart, so the difference goes negative and clamps to zero silently.
- The debug run is also **physically impossible and main doesn't notice**: `frame/sample 73 ns` exceeds `frame/call 0 ns` (a part exceeding its whole), and `adj/call 82.19 ns` exceeds the ~48 ns raw means — which is why the entire `adjusted` column is clamped to 0.0. The branch's -3 commit adds precisely these invariant checks (`frame_call > 0`, `frame_sample >= 0`, `frame_sample <= frame_call`), retries, and prints WARNING lines instead of publishing a clamp. On the branch, this run would have loudly told you the calibration was invalid.

## The branch itself

The three landed commits form a coherent ladder: one shared `#[inline(never)] run_inner` so the loop term *cancels* instead of being estimated at a different call site (-1); the slope from a low sample quantile that survives one-sided scheduler contamination (-2); and `frame_sample` as a difference of two same-N measurements so no contaminated long point can lever it negative, plus the invariant/retry machinery (-3). The chores-04 narrative and TODO resume notes are unusually complete — -4 (report only what's applied) is fully specified, and close-out mechanics (Merge non-ff, `Commits:` backfill, ff main, rebase web-claude-tweaks) are written down.

I think yesterday's "somewhat failing" feeling came from the *measurement environment* — the sandbox `--unshare-pid` spinner gotcha burned two rounds of data, and contention kept tripping the new invariant checks — not from the design. The notes leave two honest loose threads, and on one of them I have a concrete lead:

- **`d_low.min_window_ns` swinging ~8% between attempts.** The -3 formula differences `d_low.min_window_ns` against `l_low`, but the two passes have very different window shapes: the dither pass is 40 windows × 2,500 samples, while the loop-only pass is 1,000 windows × 1,000 samples. The -1 commit's own doc comment says differenced passes "must be comparable in duration or the difference is meaningless" — and it enforced that for `w_low`/`l_low`, but `d_low`'s windows are ~2.5× longer and its min is an order statistic over 40 candidates instead of 1,000. We think that asymmetry is a plausible source of both the instability and the backwards debug `frame_call` on r5-7600x; aligning the dither pass's window shape (or taking `frame_sample` from a dedicated same-shape pass) is a cheap experiment to run first.

## The bucket situation

Two separate things here:

1. **There are two band-table implementations** — `src/harness.rs` + `src/bands.rs` renders the z/p/n report you pasted; `src/band_table.rs` is the older min/p1/…/max ladder for the tprobe paths. Unifying them is already a recorded todo. The `web-claude-tweaks` commit only touches `band_table.rs`: its fixes are real but modest — `range` now uses `lowest_equivalent` instead of the raw recorded value, band means use `median_equivalent`, and it adds debug_asserts for band ordering/overlap. The harness copy has the same design but not those fixes.
2. **The strange debug table is mostly an artifact, not an indexing bug.** In debug the clock quantum (~10 ns) is coarse relative to the values, so millions of samples collapse onto a handful of lattice points (40, 41, 50, 51 ns). The assignment algorithm places each *entire equal-value bucket* into the one band containing its midpoint rank — so a single value holding 64% of samples lands wholly in "p60", and p40/p50 rows vanish. The math is doing what it was told; the told thing just produces misleading rows under a coarse lattice (that "p60" row really spans roughly p31–p95). If that bothers you, the fix is a design change — splitting an equal-value bucket's count proportionally across the bands its rank-span crosses — and deserves its own todo, not a detour in this cycle.

## How I'd proceed

1. Resume fix-calibration where the notes left off — the branch needs no rework.
2. Before -4, spend one short experiment on the window-shape asymmetry above, since -4 will demote `frame/call` to `-v` and you want the inputs stable before hiding diagnostics.
3. Then -4, close-out (Merge non-ff as planned), ff main, rebase web-claude-tweaks onto it with a real version.
4. File the proportional-band-splitting idea as a Todo tied to the existing band-table-unification entry rather than fixing it now.

The plain version: yesterday's branch is good and nearly done — the scary zero you saw this morning came from running the old code on main, and the new code would have caught and flagged it. The weird debug histogram is mostly the display rounding coarse clock ticks into a few piles, not corrupted data. I'd pick the branch back up, test one hunch about mismatched measurement windows, finish the last planned step, and ship it.

content.text:
Good instinct to poke at — but the statistics here are a bit counterintuitive, so let me separate what more points would and wouldn't buy.

## Why two points isn't as fragile as it sounds

The model being fitted is linear *by construction*: `elapsed(N) = frame_sample + N × loop_iter`, where N is the inner-loop count of the same compiled loop. There's no hypothesis that the trend "happens to be" linear — each iteration executes literally identical instructions, so total cost is a count times a unit cost, plus framing. When the model is genuinely a straight line, classical optimal-design theory says the best use of a fixed measurement budget for estimating the *slope* is to put all of it at the two extremes of the N range — interior points have less leverage and mostly just dilute the budget. So two points isn't a corner being cut; for slope precision it's actually the optimum.

The other thing to note is that each "point" is not a single reading — it's an aggregate over ~100,000 timed samples (40 windows × 2,500), with the estimator (the low quantile) chosen for robustness. The statistical spread you'd want multiple points to average away is already averaged away *within* each point, and the branch's -2 commit checked that: four different discard fractions agreed on the slope to six significant figures even under deliberate contention. Random scatter is not this measurement's problem.

## What more points *would* buy — and it's a real thing

The dominant errors here are systematic, not statistical: one-sided scheduler contamination that grows with sample duration, frequency-regime shifts, lattice bias. A systematic error that hits both points doesn't average away with repetition — and with only two points it's *invisible*: two points always fit a line perfectly, residual zero, no matter how corrupted they are. That's the legitimate weakness in your gut feeling's direction. More points can't make the slope more precise, but they can make a violated model *detectable* as curvature or misfit.

One more wrinkle worth knowing: because N_HIGH/N_LOW = 100, the slope is `(y_high − y_low)/9,900` ≈ `y_high/10,000` — it's almost entirely determined by the high point alone. So the two-point fit is nearly a one-point amortized measurement, and anything that inflates long samples specifically (which is exactly what contention does) lands straight in the slope with no way to notice. The -2 commit defends against that with the low-quantile estimator, but nothing currently *verifies* the defense worked on a given run.

## What I'd actually do

Not a multi-point *production* fit — a multi-point *diagnostic*:

- Add one or two interior points (say N = 1,000, roughly the geometric middle) measured with the same dithered low-quantile machinery, and report the residual against the two-point line. On a clean run it should be tiny; a visible bow means duration-proportional contamination got through, and that becomes another entry in the -3-style "this calibration is not to be trusted" checks — which is exactly the pattern this branch has been building.
- If the diagnostic ever shows the model failing in practice, the natural production upgrade is a Theil–Sen fit (median of pairwise slopes) over several N values — it's robust to exactly the one-sided contamination this project worries about. But I'd wait for evidence before spending calibration budget on it; calibration is ~150–200 ms and more points cost real time.

We think the interior points will confirm linearity on a quiet machine — the model has strong physical grounds — and their value is as a tripwire, not as extra averaging.

The plain version: two points is enough to *draw* the line, and here the line is guaranteed straight by how the measurement is built, so extra points wouldn't make the answer more accurate. What two points can't do is tell you when something went wrong, because two points always look like a perfect line. So the improvement isn't "fit through many points" — it's "measure one point in the middle and check it lands on the line." If it does, trust the calibration; if it doesn't, that's the alarm bell.

content.text:
The slope is `loop_per_iter_ns` — the cost of the benchmark harness's own inner-loop machinery, per iteration: the loop branch/counter plus the `black_box` that keeps the compiler from optimizing the benched call away.

Its one remaining consumer (on the fix-calibration branch) is the per-call subtraction in reported results. A recorded sample times `inner` back-to-back calls, so each per-call value is:

```
reported = raw/inner − loop_per_iter_ns − frame_sample_ns/inner
```

That's the `adj/call` in the bench header — in your release run, `adj/call = 1.47 ns` was `0.544` (loop/iter) `+ 19.514/21` (frame/sample amortized over inner=21). So the slope is subtracted at full size from *every* reported number: a 0.1 ns slope error is a 0.1 ns error in every mean and band in the table. Against ~21 ns measurements that's ~0.5%; in debug builds, where the slope is ~9 ns against ~50 ns samples, it's ~18% — the stakes are much higher there.

It had a second consumer on main — deriving `frame_call` by subtracting `N_LOW × slope` from the window pass — but that's exactly what -1 removed (it's what produced the 0.000 ns), replaced by the paired loop-only pass. The intercept of the same fit also lost its job in -3. So the two-point fit, which used to feed all three constants, now feeds only this one number.

Worth having in view for your "calibrate differently" question: the branch already invented the cleaner instrument. `l_low` (the loop-only pass) is a *direct* measurement of `N_LOW × loop_iter + per-sample loop framing` — no fit involved. The fit's remaining role is essentially to split loop cost out per-iteration, and a pair of loop-only passes at two (or more) N values could do that job with the same paired-measurement style as the other two constants, retiring the dithered two-point fit from production entirely rather than reinforcing it.

The plain version: the slope is the harness's own bookkeeping cost per loop turn, and it gets subtracted from every number the tool reports, so it must be right for the results to be right. It used to help compute three calibration numbers; after yesterday's fixes it computes only this one — which makes "should we measure it a different way" a very natural next question, and there's already a measurement style on the branch that could take over.

content.text:
## Retiring the two-point fit: better, I think — and here's the case

Measuring the slope from loop-only passes at several N values is more consistent with where the branch has already gone, and it removes real failure modes:

- **It's the same instrument as the other two constants.** After -1 and -3, `frame_call` and `frame_sample` are both differences of paired window passes over the shared `run_inner`. The slope is the last constant still coming from a different apparatus (dithered per-sample timing + extrapolation). Deriving it as `(l(N₂) − l(N₁)) / (N₂ − N₁)` makes all three constants one measurement family — same estimator (min over window means), same codegen, same contamination defense.
- **The lattice problem largely disappears.** The loop-only pass has no per-sample timer reads: one timer pair wraps a whole window of 1,000 samples, so the ~10 ns clock quantum lands once per ~50 µs window instead of once per sample — quantization error per iteration drops to the ~0.0001 ns level *before* any dither or quantile tricks. The entire negative-intercept saga from -3 was a lattice-bias problem in per-sample quantiles; this measurement style just doesn't have it.
- **Multi-point comes nearly free, which answers your reliability wish.** Loop-only windows are cheap (no timer traffic), so running N = 100, 300, 1,000, 3,000, 10,000 costs little. That gives you the linearity tripwire from earlier — residuals against the fitted line — and if you want robustness, Theil–Sen over the pairwise slopes. Interior points stop being a budget argument entirely, since you've said budget isn't the constraint.
- **Contamination defense carries over.** Min-over-window-means with short windows is exactly the estimator -1/-3 already trust; duration-proportional interference gets shed per point the same way at every N.

The honest caveat: the slope gets subtracted from *timed intervals*, and a loop-only pass measures the loop with no timer pairs interleaved. We think the per-iteration loop cost is the same in both settings — it's the identical compiled `run_inner`, and the branch's `frame_call = w_low − l_low` subtraction already leans on that same assumption — but microarchitecturally the timer read could overlap differently with loop execution. The two-point fit is worth keeping as a *diagnostic* precisely to watch for that: if the dithered-fit slope and the loop-only slope diverge persistently, that divergence is information. So: retire it from production, keep it in the `-v` alternative-fits block.

## Dithering: helping in one place, hurting in another — and yes, you're conflating two defenses

Worth pulling apart, because the two threat models get different tools:

- **Dither defends against the clock lattice, not against noise.** The timer ticks in ~10 ns quanta; without dither, a repeating loop sits at a fixed phase against that lattice and rounds the same way every time — a systematic bias that no amount of averaging removes. Dither randomizes the phase so the rounding error becomes zero-mean, and then *means* average it away. That's the whole trick, and for mean-type estimators it demonstrably works (the r5-7600x ±0.06 ns repeatability).
- **A noisy environment is a different, one-sided threat**, and dither does nothing for it — defense there comes from robust estimators (min-over-windows, low quantiles), short windows that fit between preemptions, the -3 invariant checks, and retry. So your instinct "it feels right because environments won't be quiet" is attaching dither to the wrong threat — but the conclusion (keep it) is still right, for the lattice reason.
- **Where it's actively hurting: quantile estimators.** A minimum or low quantile of dithered lattice-valued samples reads the samples that happened to round *down* — the "lattice floor." That's not noise averaging out; it's selecting for the most-biased samples, and it's exactly the ~1-quantum bias that drove the fit intercept to −1.28 ns and forced -3's redesign. Dither plus mean: friends. Dither plus min/quantile: adversaries.
- The tidy part: the redesign above resolves the tension by construction. If the slope moves to loop-only passes, the only production consumer of dithered data left is `d_low.min_window_ns` — a min over *window means*, and each window mean averages 2,500 dithered samples first, so it's on the "friends" side. The quantile-of-raw-samples estimator, the one dither fights with, retires along with the fit. The loop-only passes need no dither at all — with no per-sample timer reads there's no lattice to de-bias.

So the proposed shape is: three constants, all from paired amortized window passes; dither retained only inside the dithered window pass where means do the aggregating; two-point fit and low-quantile machinery demoted to diagnostics. That's a coherent -4-or-new-rung for the cycle, and it subsumes the window-shape-asymmetry lead from earlier (the redesign forces you to make the pass shapes comparable anyway).

The plain version: yes, switch the slope to the loop-only style — it uses the trick the branch already trusts, sidesteps the clock-granularity problem instead of fighting it, and makes "use many points" cheap, which is what you wanted for confidence. On dither: it exists to smear out the timer's coarse tick marks, not to fight a busy machine — busy-machine defense is a different mechanism that's already in place. Dither helps whenever we average, and backfires whenever we take a minimum; the redesign keeps it only where we average, so it stays helpful everywhere it remains.

message.content: Ok, let's plan the new calibration rung on fix-calibration, but I think we need to run the diagnositics everytime, we can't assume the user knows it even exists or when to do it. Thoughts?

content.text:
## On always-running the diagnostics: agree — with one distinction that keeps it sane

The distinction is **always run ≠ always print**. You're right that a diagnostic gated behind `-v` or a `calibrate` subcommand protects nobody — the user who most needs it doesn't know it exists. But printing raw residuals and alternative fits every run fails the same user a different way: numbers they can't interpret are noise, and noise trains people to ignore the block entirely.

The -3 commit already found the right pattern, we just extend it: **every check runs on every calibration; a passing check is silent; a failing check prints a WARNING in plain language.** The user needs zero prior knowledge — the tool self-checks and speaks up only when the constants shouldn't be trusted. The raw diagnostic *values* stay visible under `-v` and the `calibrate` command for the person debugging the warning.

Two design consequences fall out:

- **Checks need tolerances, not just sign tests.** The -3 invariants are exact physical impossibilities. The new ones (linearity residual, slope cross-check) are statistical, so they need thresholds set conservatively enough that a quiet machine essentially never warns — a false alarm every third run would destroy trust in the mechanism. We think validation runs on both boxes should set them empirically (e.g., several × the observed quiet-machine spread).
- **The cache must participate.** Calibration is cached (the f006b09 work), so diagnostics run only when calibration actually runs. Rules: a calibration with violations is never cached, and the cache records that its entry passed — so a cached load can honestly print nothing.

## Proposed rung plan for the branch

Insert two rungs before the existing reporting rung, which slides to -6:

- **0.22.0-4 fix: slope from multi-N loop-only passes**
  - `measure_loop_only` at an N ladder (roughly geometric: 100, 300, 1,000, 3,000, 10,000), samples-per-window scaled ~1/N so window *duration* stays roughly constant (~50–100 µs) — the -1 lesson: short windows dodge preemption, and comparability of windows is what makes min-over-windows meaningful across points.
  - production `loop_per_iter_ns` = robust fit over those points (Theil–Sen, median of pairwise slopes — matches the one-sided-contamination threat model; least squares is fine as a logged comparison).
  - align the dither pass's window shape with the loop-only pass at N_LOW (fixes the ~8% `min_window_ns` loose thread; `frame_sample = d_low.min_window − l_low` finally differences comparable things).
  - keep the dithered two-point fit computed and logged, no longer a production input.
- **0.22.0-5 feat: always-on calibration self-checks**
  - linearity residual check over the N ladder; slope cross-check (loop-only slope vs dithered-fit slope); the -3 physical invariants stay.
  - all checks run every calibration, silent on pass, plain-language WARNING on fail, folded into the existing `violations` retry/report machinery.

content.text:
Yes — and the calibration data we already collect is most of the way to it. This is a good idea worth its own spot in the ladder. Let me lay out what "noisy" is measurable as, what the number should be, and one honest caveat about what a calibration-time grade can and can't promise.

## The signals we already have (or get cheaply)

Interference has a distinctive signature — one-sided, sporadic, duration-proportional — and the calibration passes are effectively a census of it:

- **Disturbed-sample fraction.** From the dither passes: the low quantile establishes the clean floor; count the fraction of samples above, say, floor × 1.5. On a quiet machine that's well under 1%; your pasted debug run shows ~0.01% of samples out at 5–36 µs against a 40 ns floor. "2.3% of calibration samples were disturbed" is directly meaningful.
- **Clean-window availability.** Fraction of windows whose mean sits within tolerance of the min window (the existing `window_spread` / `median_window` data, restated). This measures whether min-over-windows had clean material to find — the thing that actually decides whether the constants are trustworthy.
- **Estimator divergence.** The -2 finding in reusable form: under a continuous competitor the `fast`-windows mean pulls away from the sample quantiles. That divergence specifically detects *continuous* load, which the disturbed-fraction census under-reports.
- **Repeatability — the gold standard.** Since budget isn't the constraint: run the calibration twice and difference the constants. That's a direct, assumption-free uncertainty estimate — "frame/sample repeats to ±0.08 ns" — and it catches anything the per-pass statistics miss. The retry machinery from -3 already half-builds this.
- **Drift check (cheap bonus).** Re-run the N_LOW loop-only pass at the end of calibration and compare to the start; a shift means frequency/thermal drift mid-calibration, a different disease than preemption and worth naming separately in the warning.

## What the number should be

A grade must be interpretable without a manual, so I'd print one always-on line with a letter grade plus the evidence, and reserve WARNING for the bad end:

```
environment       A  (disturbed 0.3%, clean windows 96%, repeatability ±0.06 ns)
```

- The **letter** comes from the worst of the individual signals (a noisy environment only needs to fail one way), with thresholds set empirically from quiet-machine runs on both boxes — same calibration philosophy as the -5 warning thresholds.
- The **repeatability figure in ns** is the number I'd emphasize over any unitless score: it states the consequence ("constants are good to ±X ns") rather than an abstract score, and it's honest — users can weigh ±0.1 ns against their measured 20 ns effect themselves.
- Grades C and below additionally emit the plain-language WARNING you asked for: "environment is noisy; calibration constants and results below are unreliable."

This slots naturally into the ladder as an extension of **-5 (always-on self-checks)** — the grade is exactly the user-facing synthesis of those checks — with the -6 reporting rung deciding the final line format. I'd keep it one rung; splitting grade from checks would have the two rungs editing the same code.

## The honest caveat

A calibration-time grade certifies the ~200 ms calibration window, but the bench then runs for seconds — the environment can sour after a clean calibration, and that noise lands in the *results*, not the constants. So the calibration grade is necessary but not sufficient, and we shouldn't let the line imply full coverage. The good news: the same census transfers — the bench histogram's own tail (fraction of samples beyond a floor multiple, the existing `suspended_s` warning) can grade the run itself. I'd scope run-time grading as a separate Todo entry rather than stretching this cycle; the calibration grade plus the existing invariants is already a big step up in trustworthiness.

The plain version: the calibration already sees every interference spike that hits it — we just haven't been counting them. So we count them, check the numbers agree when measured twice, and print one small report card after every calibration: a letter grade plus "the constants repeat to within such-and-such." Quiet machine, grade A, no drama; noisy machine, a clear warning that says don't trust this run. The one limit is that the report card covers the calibration moment, not the whole benchmark that follows — grading the benchmark itself the same way is a good follow-up project.

content.content:
# Cycle protocol

This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.

The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
the conversation — code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
equivalents — this project's manifest is recorded in
[versioning.md](versioning.md).

## Cycles

A cycle has three phases:

- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's
  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
  it and starts at `-1` — see
  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
  cycle:
  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
    and the suffix scheme are project-specific — see
    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
    statement + plan ladder).
  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the
  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
  needs; each runs through the
  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's
  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
    `## Done`.
  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
    [chores section](#chores-sections).
  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
    changed.

A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
result must always be published at close-out. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
warrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`
Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
for the local-ladder mechanics.

## Chores sections

A **chores section** is a `##` section in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
chores file.

The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. **Each work commit
then appends its own As-built rung + narrative note as it
lands** — the chores record is built up per commit, not held
back and written all at once at close-out; close-out only
*finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
`## In Progress` block). The `Commits:` line is backfilled
later, once the commit is permanent (see
[Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).

### Commits backfill

A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
records, by SHA — but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
squash rewrites it on the way. So:

- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands —
  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
  invalidate.

Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
section records multiple commits (a merge non-ff close-out) —
with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's `# References`
(format in AGENTS.md
[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
`git log --grep "<title>"`.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma — a
**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
SHA must be permanent.

## Preparation

The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
setup (a lightweight cycle omits it — see
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):

- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
  project-specific — see [versioning.md](versioning.md).
- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:
  - A **bold title line** — that will be the chores
    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.
  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed
  - A **plan ladder**.
- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)** —
  append a `##` header with the title it records — the
  cycle's anticipated close-out title.

## Work-N

The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …)
implement the change. As many as needed:

- Each commit runs through the
  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
  visibility).
- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
  [Pushing](#pushing)).
- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
  scope grows enough (see
  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).

## Close-out

The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping
only — the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not
what happens post-squash:

- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a
  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.
- **Finalize the chores section** (opened during Preparation
  and grown per commit — see [Chores sections](#chores-sections)):
  - The problem statement is already the chores intro (written
    when the section was opened) and the plan ladder is already
    the `### As-built ladder` (a rung appended per commit), so
    close-out only *finalizes*, it does not cut-and-paste.
  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title if the
    cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor back-reference.
  - Add any `### design subsections`; optional `### Outcome`
    notes.
  - Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block with
    `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).

Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time —
see [Pushing](#pushing).

## Numbering

Each commit's phase is encoded in the version suffix — `-0`
Preparation, `-1`/`-2`/… Work, bare `X.Y.Z` Close-out,
recursively for sub-cycles. The full scheme — disambiguation,
nesting, optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
format, and the per-phase bump — lives in
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering), which is the
single source of truth for this repo's versioning.

## Per-commit flow

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
through:

1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
   root).
2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
   for the loop-and-squash technique).
3. **Flip this commit `(current)` → `(done)`** in `## In
   Progress` — before the cargo cycle and the commit.
4. **Validate the artifact** — a medium-specific step, skip-able
   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
   example the cargo cycle is:
   1. `cargo fmt`
   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
   3. `cargo test`

3. `cargo test`
   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;
   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
   changes and we iterate until complete.
6. **Write the commit description** — see
   [Commit description](#commit-description).
7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
8. **Commit.** `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R .` for
   the work repo, `-R .claude` for the bot repo (`-R` last
   keeps the verb visible):

   ```
   jj commit -m \
   "<type>: <short description>" \
   -m "<intro paragraph>

   - file1: gist
   - file2: gist

   ochid: /.claude/<chid>" \
   -R .
   ```

**Two overrides apply:**

- **Deviation or question** — any time the work deviates
  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
  surface it; don't push through.
- **ESC-ESC** — the user can interrupt at any point to pull
  a review or question forward.

## Commit description

[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):

```
<type>: <short description>
```

Titles carry **no trailing `(<version>)` suffix**. The
version-of-record — where it lives and its bump cadence, see
[versioning.md](versioning.md) — is useful for confirming
you're running the version you're testing, not a per-commit
title marker. We think per-commit version-in-title is
unstable on large projects: many changes are in flight
simultaneously, and a
version is only stable once merged into the main repo — so
titles don't carry one.

### Title

- ≤50 chars total.
- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
  `docs`, `chore`.
- Favor terse phrasings.
- **Distinct per step** — each of a cycle's commits gets its
  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the
  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
  AGENTS.md
  [Conventional-commit shape](../AGENTS.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).

### Body

[Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets),
wrap ≤72. Bullet content differs per repo:

- **Work-repo body**: file-by-file. One bullet per file
  changed (file plus a one-line gist). Sub-bullets for
  files with multiple distinct changes:

  ```
  - path/to/file1
    - first distinct change
    - second distinct change, wrapping to next line
       with continuation indented 5
  ```

  The file-by-file list is the source of truth for the
  cycle's mechanical change record. Chores carries the
  narrative + design, not a copy of it. Promote any
  "why" beyond one sentence to a chores `###` subsection.

- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: bullets describe
  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.

### Trailer

`ochid:` as the last line of the body — see
[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](../AGENTS.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
in AGENTS.md for the convention.

For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows; the
hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.

## Reviewing changes

Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
editor (Zed, VSCode); jj commands are for terminal:

- `jj diff` — working-copy diff (uncommitted)
- `jj diff -r @-` — diff of the previous commit
- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>` — any two revisions
- `jj show -r <X>` — description + diff for one rev

Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit — that marks
it mutable and shifts `@`; use `jj diff -r @-` or
`jj show -r @-`.

See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
close-out squash recipe and recovery; revset primitives
are in [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets).

## Pushing

1	//! Apparatus-overhead calibration, dithered and amortized.
2	//!
3	//! Three constants, from three measurement passes:
4	//!
5	//! - **Dithered two-point fit** (low sample quantile at `N_LOW` /
6	//!   `N_HIGH`, random sub-quantum phase dither per sample) gives
7	//!   the slope → `loop_per_iter_ns`, subtracted per call.
8	//! - **Window pass** and **loop-only pass** (min over amortized
9	//!   window means at `N_LOW`, identical but for the per-sample
10	//!   timer pair): their difference is `frame_call_ns`, the full
11	//!   call-to-call cost of taking a sample — sizes the experiment,
12	//!   never subtracted (most of it sits outside recorded
13	//!   intervals).
14	//! - **Dither `N_LOW` window minimum minus the loop-only pass**
15	//!   gives `frame_sample_ns`, the in-interval timer-pair slice a
16	//!   recorded sample actually contains, subtracted per sample.
17	//!
18	//! Every pass drives the same [`run_inner`], so the loop term
19	//! cancels exactly in both subtractions instead of being
20	//! estimated at a different call site.
21	//!
22	//! The slope and the intercept come from *different* estimators
23	//! on purpose. A low quantile parks both fit points on the clock
24	//! lattice floor; in the slope that shared ~1-quantum bias
25	//! cancels, but in an extrapolated intercept it lands undiluted —
26	//! enough to drive the intercept negative on a quiet machine
27	//! (r5-7600x: fit intercept -1.2828 ns against a paired 8.23 ns,
28	//! three runs). So the intercept is instead a difference of two
29	//! same-`N_LOW` measurements, which cannot be levered by a
30	//! contaminated long point.
31	//!
32	//! Dither makes the ~10 ns clock quantum a zero-mean error that
33	//! averages away in means (validated on r5-7600x: `frame_sample`
34	//! 8.23 / 8.25 / 8.29 ns, a 0.062 ns spread, within a frequency
35	//! regime). See notes/design.md#dithering-random-phase-injection,
36	//! notes/design.md#timer-overhead-in-interval-vs-call-to-call and
37	//! notes/chores/chores-04.md#one-sided-contamination-and-the-two-point-fit.

40	use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

45	/// boost to ramp before the first measurement.

48	/// Attempts before a physically impossible calibration is
49	/// reported rather than retried. Interference is transient, so a
50	/// retry usually lands on a quieter moment; a persistent
51	/// violation is a real problem the user needs to see.
52	pub const CAL_MAX_ATTEMPTS: u32 = 3;
53	
54	/// Inner-loop count for the low-N calibration point.
55	pub const N_LOW: u64 = 100;
56	
57	/// Inner-loop count for the high-N calibration point. A wide spread
58	/// (`N_HIGH / (N_HIGH - N_LOW) ≈ 1.01`) keeps noise amplification on
59	/// the fitted intercept small.
60	pub const N_HIGH: u64 = 10_000;

62	/// Samples per window in the call-to-call and loop-only passes at

64	/// ~0.01 ns at a ~10 ns quantum.
65	///
66	/// - Lowered from 10,000 with the window count raised to match,
67	///   leaving the total budget unchanged. Window *duration* is

72	///   containing it. Shorter windows fit between preemptions.
73	/// - The two passes are differenced, so their windows must be

75	pub const W_LOW_SAMPLES: u64 = 1_000;
76	
77	/// Windows in the call-to-call and loop-only passes; the minimum
78	/// is kept. The min sheds windows inflated by preemption or a
79	/// frequency dip while staying amortized (each candidate is

81	pub const W_LOW_WINDOWS: u64 = 1_000;

83	/// Dither span in neutral spin iterations (~0.4-0.5 ns each →

86	/// lattice, making the quantization error zero-mean (see

88	pub const DITHER_SPAN: u64 = 64;
89	
90	/// Dithered-fit windows per point (each yields one window mean;

102	/// Dithered-fit samples per window at [`N_HIGH`] (samples are

120	/// Candidate discard fractions for the low-quantile estimator:

133	
134	/// Index into [`DITHER_LOW_Q`] selecting the discard fraction

137	/// - Only the slope. The fit's intercept carries the quantile's
138	///   ~1-quantum lattice bias undiluted, where the slope cancels

140	pub const DITHER_PROD_Q: usize = 2;

142	/// Xorshift64* PRNG for dither lengths. No external dep; phase
143	/// randomization needs rough uniformity, not statistical rigor.
144	struct XorShift64(u64);
145	
146	impl XorShift64 {
147	    /// Next pseudo-random u64.
148	    fn next(&mut self) -> u64 {
149	        let mut x = self.0;
150	        x ^= x >> 12;
151	        x ^= x << 25;
152	        x ^= x >> 27;
153	        self.0 = x;
154	        x.wrapping_mul(0x2545_F491_4F6C_DD1D)
155	    }
156	}

158	/// Sub-quantum phase dither: a random 0..[`DITHER_SPAN`] neutral
159	/// spin, run *outside* the timed interval before each sample.
160	/// Used by calibration and by the harness sample seam.
161	pub struct Dither(XorShift64);
162	
163	impl Dither {
164	    /// New dither source, seeded from wall-clock nanos (any

175	    /// next sample's phase on the clock lattice.

177	    pub fn spin(&mut self) {
178	        let r = self.0.next() % DITHER_SPAN;

185	    /// randomness (e.g. the harness's block sleep lengths).

234	#[derive(Debug)]
235	pub struct Overhead {
236	    /// Call-to-call cost of taking one sample (full timer-pair
237	    /// apparatus cost, clock-read latencies included), in ns —
238	    /// the window pass minus the loop-only pass. Sizes the
239	    /// experiment ([`crate::harness`]'s `pick_inner`); most of it
240	    /// sits *outside* recorded intervals, so it is never
241	    /// subtracted from reported values. Clamped at 0, with a
242	    /// warning, if the two passes disagree.
243	    pub frame_call_ns: f64,
244	    /// In-interval timer-pair slice a recorded sample contains,
245	    /// in ns — the dithered `N_LOW` window minimum minus the
246	    /// loop-only pass, both amortized per-sample costs over the
247	    /// same [`run_inner`]. Subtracted per sample (amortized by
248	    /// `inner`); see [`Overhead::adjust_per_call_ns`].
249	    pub frame_sample_ns: f64,

251	    /// in ns — the dithered fit's slope. Subtracted per call.
252	    /// Also the frequency-regime fingerprint (repeats to 5

254	    pub loop_per_iter_ns: f64,

256	    /// Preserved for `-v` logging and cache provenance.

275	impl Overhead {
276	    /// Per-call apparatus overhead subtracted from reported values,
277	    /// in ns: the amortized loop cost plus the in-interval framing
278	    /// slice amortized by `inner`.
279	    ///

290	
291	impl Bench for EmptyBench {
292	    fn name(&self) -> &str {
293	        "empty"
294	    }
295	
296	    fn step(&mut self) -> u64 {

301	/// The inner loop, as one compiled copy shared by every
302	/// calibration pass.
303	///
304	/// - `#[inline(never)]` is load-bearing: `frame_call_ns` is a
305	///   difference of two passes, so any per-call-site codegen
306	///   difference in this loop lands in the result at full size.
307	///   One copy makes it cancel instead. See
308	///   notes/chores/chores-04.md#call-site-codegen-and-the-frame_call-subtraction.
309	/// - The call itself costs one call per *sample*, not per
310	///   iteration, so it does not enter `loop_per_iter_ns`; it is a
311	///   constant present in every pass, and cancels too.
312	#[inline(never)]
313	fn run_inner(bench: &mut EmptyBench, inner: u64) {
314	    for _ in 0..inner {
315	        black_box(bench.step());
316	    }
317	}
318	
319	/// Calibrate, retrying while the result is physically impossible.
320	///
321	/// - A violation (see [`Overhead::violations`]) means interference
322	///   corrupted the run, not that the apparatus is slow, so another
323	///   attempt on a quieter moment is the right response.
324	/// - After [`CAL_MAX_ATTEMPTS`] the last attempt is returned with
325	///   its violations attached, for the caller to report. A clamped
326	///   constant is never passed off as a measurement.
327	pub fn calibrate() -> Overhead {
328	    let mut last = calibrate_once();
329	    for attempt in 2..=CAL_MAX_ATTEMPTS {
330	        if last.violations.is_empty() {
331	            return last;
332	        }
333	        log::warn!(
334	            "calibration attempt {} of {CAL_MAX_ATTEMPTS} was physically impossible \
335	             ({}); retrying",
336	            attempt - 1,
337	            last.violations.join("; "),
338	        );
339	        last = calibrate_once();
340	    }
341	    last
342	}
343	
344	/// One calibration pass: the dithered two-point measurement plus
345	/// the call-to-call and loop-only window passes. Blocks for
346	/// ~150-200 ms on a typical modern x86; logs raw points and the
347	/// alternative fits at debug level.
348	fn calibrate_once() -> Overhead {
349	    let mut bench = EmptyBench;
350	    let mut dither = Dither::new();
351	    let cal_start = Instant::now();
352	    for _ in 0..CAL_WARMUP {
353	        black_box(bench.step());
354	    }
355	
356	    let d_low = dither_measure(&mut dither, DITHER_WINDOWS, DITHER_LOW_SAMPLES, N_LOW);
357	    let d_high = dither_measure(&mut dither, DITHER_WINDOWS, DITHER_HIGH_SAMPLES, N_HIGH);
358	    log_dither_point("d_low", &d_low);
359	    log_dither_point("d_high", &d_high);
360	    log_alt_fits(&d_low, &d_high);
361	
362	    // Call-to-call: two window passes at N_LOW differing only in
363	    // the per-sample timer pair, so the loop term cancels in the
364	    // subtraction rather than being estimated from the dithered
365	    // slope (a different call site, and in an unoptimized build a
366	    // ~12% different loop — see
367	    // notes/chores/chores-04.md#call-site-codegen-and-the-frame_call-subtraction).
368	    let w_low = measure_window(&mut bench, W_LOW_WINDOWS, W_LOW_SAMPLES, N_LOW);
369	    let l_low = measure_loop_only(&mut bench, W_LOW_WINDOWS, W_LOW_SAMPLES, N_LOW);
370	    let frame_call_raw = w_low - l_low;
371	
372	    // The slope still comes from the two-point fit over a low
373	    // sample quantile: interference is one-sided and lands hardest
374	    // on the long N_HIGH samples, so only the low tail is
375	    // uncontaminated.
376	    let (fit_intercept, loop_per_iter_ns) = two_point_fit(
377	        d_low.low_q_ns[DITHER_PROD_Q],
378	        d_high.low_q_ns[DITHER_PROD_Q],
379	    );
380	
381	    // frame_sample is *not* taken from that intercept: it is a
382	    // difference of two same-N measurements over the same
383	    // run_inner, so no long point can lever it negative. Both
384	    // terms are amortized per-sample costs, min over windows.
385	    let frame_sample_raw = d_low.min_window_ns - l_low;
386	    log::debug!(
387	        "frame_sample: paired={frame_sample_raw:.4} ns (d_low_minwin={:.4}, l_low={l_low:.4}), \
388	         fit-intercept={fit_intercept:.4} ns",
389	        d_low.min_window_ns,
390	    );
391	    log::debug!(
392	        "frame_call: paired={frame_call_raw:.4} ns (w_low={w_low:.4}, l_low={l_low:.4}), \
393	         slope-based={:.4} ns",
394	        w_low - N_LOW as f64 * loop_per_iter_ns,
395	    );
396	
397	    // Physical plausibility. These are not statistical tests: each
398	    // one is a statement that cannot be false of a real apparatus,
399	    // so a failure means the measurement is invalid, not unlucky.
400	    let mut violations = Vec::new();
401	    if frame_call_raw <= 0.0 {
402	        violations.push(format!(
403	            "frame/call is non-positive ({frame_call_raw:.4} ns; w_low={w_low:.4}, \
404	             l_low={l_low:.4}): taking a sample cannot cost nothing"
405	        ));
406	    }
407	    if frame_sample_raw < 0.0 {
408	        violations.push(format!(
409	            "frame/sample is negative ({frame_sample_raw:.4} ns; d_low_minwin={:.4}, \
410	             l_low={l_low:.4}): a timed interval cannot be shorter than the loop it contains",
411	            d_low.min_window_ns,
412	        ));
413	    }
414	    if frame_sample_raw > frame_call_raw {
415	        violations.push(format!(
416	            "frame/sample ({frame_sample_raw:.4} ns) exceeds frame/call \
417	             ({frame_call_raw:.4} ns): the timer cost inside the interval cannot \
418	             exceed the whole timer cost"
419	        ));
420	    }
421	
422	    let frame_call_ns = frame_call_raw.max(0.0);
423	    let frame_sample_ns = frame_sample_raw.max(0.0);
424	
425	    Overhead {
426	        frame_call_ns,
427	        frame_sample_ns,
428	        loop_per_iter_ns,
429	        cal_w_low_ns: w_low,
430	        cal_l_low_ns: l_low,
431	        cal_d_low: d_low,
432	        cal_d_high: d_high,
433	        cal_duration: cal_start.elapsed(),
434	        violations,
435	    }
436	}
437	
438	/// Measure one dithered point: `windows` windows of `samples`
439	/// samples at the given `inner`, each sample preceded by a random
440	/// sub-quantum [`Dither::spin`] outside the timed interval.
441	fn dither_measure(dither: &mut Dither, windows: u64, samples: u64, inner: u64) -> DitherPoint {
442	    let mut bench = EmptyBench;
443	    let mut all: Vec<u64> = Vec::with_capacity((windows * samples) as usize);
444	    let mut window_means: Vec<f64> = Vec::with_capacity(windows as usize);
445	    for _ in 0..windows {
446	        let mut sum: u128 = 0;
447	        for _ in 0..samples {
448	            dither.spin();
449	            let start = Instant::now();
450	            run_inner(&mut bench, inner);
451	            let e = start.elapsed().as_nanos() as u64;
452	            sum += u128::from(e);
453	            all.push(e);
454	        }
455	        window_means.push(sum as f64 / samples as f64);
456	    }
457	
458	    all.sort_unstable();
459	    let n = all.len();
460	    let mean_ns = all.iter().map(|&v| v as f64).sum::<f64>() / n as f64;
461	    let n99 = (n as f64 * 0.99).ceil() as usize;
462	    let mean_p99_ns = all[..n99].iter().map(|&v| v as f64).sum::<f64>() / n99 as f64;
463	
464	    window_means.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| a.total_cmp(b));
465	    let median_window_ns = window_means[window_means.len() / 2];
466	    let window_spread_ns = window_means[window_means.len() - 1] - window_means[0];
467	    let fast = (DITHER_FAST_WINDOWS as usize).clamp(1, window_means.len());
468	    let mean_fast_ns = window_means[..fast].iter().sum::<f64>() / fast as f64;
469	
470	    let mut low_q_ns = [0.0; DITHER_LOW_Q.len()];
471	    for (slot, frac) in low_q_ns.iter_mut().zip(DITHER_LOW_Q) {
472	        let idx = ((n as f64 * frac) as usize).min(n - 1);
473	        *slot = all[idx] as f64;
474	    }
475	
476	    DitherPoint {
477	        mean_ns,
478	        mean_p99_ns,
479	        mean_fast_ns,
480	        low_q_ns,
481	        min_window_ns: window_means[0],
482	        median_window_ns,
483	        window_spread_ns,
484	        min_ns: all[0],
485	    }
486	}
487	
488	/// Amortized per-sample cost at a given `inner`: each window times
489	/// `samples` complete samples (timer pair around an `inner`-iteration
490	/// loop — the exact shape the harness takes one at a time) and
491	/// divides by the count, so quantization error is q/samples; the
492	/// minimum over `windows` windows is returned, in ns.
493	fn measure_window(bench: &mut EmptyBench, windows: u64, samples: u64, inner: u64) -> f64 {
494	    let mut min_ns = f64::INFINITY;
495	    for _ in 0..windows {
496	        let window = Instant::now();
497	        for _ in 0..samples {
498	            let start = Instant::now();
499	            run_inner(bench, inner);
500	            black_box(start.elapsed());
501	        }
502	        let per_sample = window.elapsed().as_nanos() as f64 / samples as f64;
503	        if per_sample < min_ns {
504	            min_ns = per_sample;
505	        }
506	    }
507	    min_ns
508	}
509	
510	/// [`measure_window`] with the per-sample timer pair removed: the
511	/// loop's own cost per `inner` iterations, same window shape, same
512	/// min-over-windows estimator, same [`run_inner`].
513	///
514	/// - Paired with [`measure_window`], the difference is the
515	///   call-to-call framing cost with the loop term cancelled
516	///   exactly — no fitted slope, no second call site.
517	fn measure_loop_only(bench: &mut EmptyBench, windows: u64, samples: u64, inner: u64) -> f64 {
518	    let mut min_ns = f64::INFINITY;
519	    for _ in 0..windows {
520	        let window = Instant::now();
521	        for _ in 0..samples {
522	            run_inner(bench, inner);
523	        }
524	        let per_sample = window.elapsed().as_nanos() as f64 / samples as f64;
525	        if per_sample < min_ns {
526	            min_ns = per_sample;
527	        }
528	    }
529	    min_ns
530	}
531	
532	/// Two-point linear fit over the [`N_LOW`] / [`N_HIGH`] pair,
533	/// shared by the production fit, the alternative-fit logging, and
534	/// the `calibrate` command's diagnostic output. Returns
535	/// `(intercept_ns, slope_ns)`; the slope clamps to 0 when the
536	/// points invert, and the intercept is left unclamped (a negative
537	/// value is itself a diagnostic signal).
538	pub fn two_point_fit(low_ns: f64, high_ns: f64) -> (f64, f64) {
539	    let slope = if high_ns > low_ns {
540	        (high_ns - low_ns) / (N_HIGH - N_LOW) as f64
541	    } else {
542	        0.0
543	    };
544	    (low_ns - N_LOW as f64 * slope, slope)
545	}
546	
547	/// Debug-log one dithered point's aggregates.
548	fn log_dither_point(name: &str, p: &DitherPoint) {
549	    log::debug!(
550	        "dither {name}: mean={:.4} p99mean={:.4} fast={:.4} medwin={:.4} spread={:.4} min={} ns",
551	        p.mean_ns,
552	        p.mean_p99_ns,
553	        p.mean_fast_ns,
554	        p.median_window_ns,
555	        p.window_spread_ns,
556	        p.min_ns,
557	    );
558	}
559	
560	/// Debug-log the alternative fits (full / p99 / fast / medwin) so
561	/// estimator agreement stays observable run to run; `fast` is the
562	/// production fit. Under contention the others go negative while
563	/// `fast` should not — that divergence is the diagnostic.
564	fn log_alt_fits(d_low: &DitherPoint, d_high: &DitherPoint) {
565	    for (kind, low, high) in fit_candidates(d_low, d_high) {
566	        let (intercept, slope) = two_point_fit(low, high);
567	        log::debug!(
568	            "dither fit({kind}): in-interval framing={intercept:.4} ns, loop_per_iter={slope:.6} ns"
569	        );
570	    }
571	}
572	
573	/// Every aggregation the two points can be fitted through, as
574	/// `(label, low, high)` — the single list behind both the `-v`
575	/// debug log and the `calibrate` command's stdout block, so the
576	/// two can't drift.
577	///
578	/// - The means come first, then one entry per [`DITHER_LOW_Q`]
579	///   discard fraction. The production fit is the `lowq` entry at
580	///   [`DITHER_PROD_Q`].
581	pub fn fit_candidates(d_low: &DitherPoint, d_high: &DitherPoint) -> Vec<(String, f64, f64)> {
582	    let mut out = vec![
583	        ("full".to_string(), d_low.mean_ns, d_high.mean_ns),
584	        ("p99".to_string(), d_low.mean_p99_ns, d_high.mean_p99_ns),
585	        ("fast".to_string(), d_low.mean_fast_ns, d_high.mean_fast_ns),
586	        (
587	            "medwin".to_string(),
588	            d_low.median_window_ns,
589	            d_high.median_window_ns,
590	        ),
591	    ];
592	    for (i, frac) in DITHER_LOW_Q.iter().enumerate() {
593	        out.push((
594	            format!("lowq{:.1}%", frac * 100.0),
595	            d_low.low_q_ns[i],
596	            d_high.low_q_ns[i],
597	        ));
598	    }
599	    out
600	}

## fix: calibration robust to codegen and noise

Commits:

Two calibration constants are derived by differencing or
extrapolating measurements that don't share their assumptions,
and both fail in the same direction: a plausible-looking number
that is silently wrong. `frame_call_ns` (-1) subtracts terms
measured at two call sites; `frame_sample_ns` (-2) extrapolates
a fit whose long point absorbs far more one-sided interference
than its short one. Neither failure is noise, so neither
averages away with more runs.

### As-built ladder

Rungs are appended as commits land; each carries its commit
ref, backfilled one push after the commit is permanent.

- [[N]] 0.22.0-1 fix: pair frame/call against a loop-only pass
- [[N]] 0.22.0-2 fix: fit frame/sample from a low sample quantile
- [[N]] 0.22.0-3 fix: derive frame/sample without extrapolating
- [[N]] 0.22.0-4 fix: report only what is applied to results
- [[N]] 0.22.0 fix: calibration robust to codegen and noise

### -1: frame/call across two call sites

`frame_call_ns` was a difference of two passes that measured
different code: a window mean from `measure_window`, minus
`N_LOW * loop_per_iter_ns` where the slope came from the dithered
fit at a different call site. The same source loop compiles
differently at the two sites, and that difference lands in the
result at full size — `frame/call` reported a clamped
`0.000 ns` in an unoptimized build and was ~30% low in release.
Fix: a `measure_loop_only` pass beside `measure_window`,
identical but for the per-sample timer pair, with both (and the
dithered pass) driving one shared `#[inline(never)] run_inner`,
so `frame_call = w_low - l_low` cancels the loop term exactly
instead of estimating it. The retired slope-based derivation
stays as a debug-level cross-check: the two agree only when
every pass measures the same loop, so disagreement is now the
alarm that was missing. Both `.max(0.0)` clamps — `frame_call`'s
and the older `frame_sample` one — now warn before clamping,
since a clamp is what let a broken model read as a plausible
`0.000 ns` in the first place.

### Call-site codegen and the frame_call subtraction

Found from a debug-build run reporting `frame/call 0.000 ns`
(3900X, 2026-07-24). The mechanism is general, so it is worth
recording past the fix.

`frame_call_ns` is a small quantity (tens of ns) extracted by
subtracting two much larger ones (hundreds to ~1000 ns). Both
terms contain the same `inner`-iteration empty loop, so the
subtraction only works if the loop term is *identical* in both.
It wasn't:

- Measured at the window-pass call site, the loop cost 742.8 ns
  per 100 iterations; at the dither-pass call site, the
  identical source loop cost 833.7 ns. That is 0.91 ns/iter,
  **12%**, from `opt-level=0` codegen alone (nothing inlines,
  and the two sites got different stack layouts).
- The inversion in one line: the window pass's *complete*
  call-to-call cost (781.8) came in below the dither site's
  *bare* loop with no timer at all (833.7).
- So `w_low - N_LOW * slope` = 781.8 - 856.9 = -75.1, and
  `.max(0.0)` turned a broken model into a plausible-looking
  `0.000 ns` — which then fed `pick_inner` through
  `frame_call_ns.max(1.0)` and mis-sized `inner` for the whole
  run.

Ruled out along the way, each by direct measurement:

- **Frequency ramp / pass order** — running the window pass
  before the dither passes instead of after changed nothing
  (loop-only 742.8 vs 741.1; window 782.4 vs 781.8).
- **The dither spin** — in-interval mean with spin 947.2 vs
  without 949.2. The spin adds ~210 ns to call-to-call and 0 to
  the interval, exactly as designed.
- **The sample `Vec` push** — 880.5 vs 884.9.
- `.as_nanos()` costs ~98 ns per sample in an unoptimized
  build, which is why the dither pass is the wall-clock
  expensive one; it sits outside the timed interval, so it
  biases nothing.

Release hid it rather than escaping it. At 0.679 ns/iter the
same 12% is ~8 ns across `N_LOW`, which merely biased
`frame/call` low (34-46 ns reported, 49-54 ns after the fix)
instead of driving it negative. We think any calibration
constant derived by differencing two passes is exposed this
way, and the general defense is the one applied here: one
compiled copy of the measured code, one estimator, and a
second independent derivation retained as a running
cross-check.

### -2: frame/sample from a low sample quantile

The production fit now takes, at each point, the minimum sample
remaining after discarding the fastest 1% — a low quantile
rather than a trimmed mean. `DITHER_WINDOWS` rises 20 -> 40 with
per-window sample counts halved, leaving the total budget
unchanged.

The first attempt took the mean of the fastest 10% of *window
means*, on the reasoning that a window mean keeps dither's
quantization cancellation while the tail selection sheds
contamination. It failed, and the failure is instructive:
window-level tail selection assumes interference is sporadic
enough that some window escapes. Against a continuous
competitor none does — an `N_HIGH` window is 250 x ~85 us
~= 21 ms, so every window is hit, and the fastest of 40 came in
at 142,644 ns against a 76,573 ns sample floor. It scored
*worse* than the mean it replaced (-592.6 vs -465.3). The same
duration-proportional argument that condemns the `N_HIGH` point
condemns any window long enough to contain it; individual
samples are the only unit short enough to slip between
preemptions. The estimator is kept as the `fast` diagnostic
because its divergence from the quantiles measures contamination.

Discarding the bottom 1% rather than taking the strict minimum

1. Unit scaling in report columns (`us`/`ms`) — per-row
   auto-scale so columns stay eyeball-comparable (bands are
   monotonic, so a row's first/last/mean share a magnitude),
   or `--units ns|auto` for script-stable output; needs
   `--decimals` landed first (`3.18 ms` vs `3 ms`); candidate
   `-4` for the report-options cycle.
2. Trimmed core stats: `mean/stdev p10-p90` report row,
   additional to (never replacing) `mean` / `mean min-p99`;
   trim bounds possibly configurable (`--trim p10:p90`?) —
   the full mean wobbles ~±1.4% with the run's mode mix while
   the core plateau is ~±0.2% stable, so the trimmed row is
   the run-to-run comparable number. Boundary sensitivity
   (see [[57]]): window edges in the mode-mix smear inherit
   its wobble (p50-p60 ±0.05% vs p40-p50 ~1%), so also
   consider a dominant-*mode* statistic (peak-density region,
   bottom-count-independent) [[57]]
3. Find and label the interference crossover — the band where
   the tail stops measuring the code and starts measuring the
   machine. Not to hide it: to *name* it, because that is the
   signal TProbe exists to surface (the OS swapping, a drive
   stalling, anything not caused by the code under test).
   - Locate it from the data rather than fixing it at a
     percentile: the giveaway is the band `range` exploding
     (min-now 0.21.0, 3900X: `n3` range 3.0 ns -> `n4` range
     200.4 ns), not a chosen p99.
   - The crossover moves with the bench. A counting argument
     places it: interference arrives at a *rate*, so it can
     only contaminate so many samples. That run's `n2` held
     838,635 of 8,059,469 samples over 5 s = ~168,000/s, and
     nothing in the OS runs at that rate, so `n2` is code. The
     `n4`+ bands total ~1,500/s — timer-interrupt territory.
   - So report the above-crossover count as an **interference
     rate**, and consider surfacing whether the run was quiet
     enough to trust. Calibration wants exactly this signal
     (see [[61]]); a contaminated run is currently only
     detectable by squinting at band ranges.
   - Pairs with the trimmed-core-stats entry above: that one
     needs a defensible upper bound, and this is how to find
     one per run instead of hardcoding p99.
4. Upstream the ladder commit-ref convention to
   `../vc-template-x1`: In Progress ladder rungs (and the
   chores As-built rungs) carry a prepended `[[N]]`
   commit-ref placeholder, backfilled as each commit
   becomes permanent — template's cycle-protocol.md,
   AGENTS.md, and TODO.md example need the shape; that
   repo has its own approval/push flow
5. Investigate: suspend gap missing from samples. A 0.13.5
   `--no-inhibit` suspend test detected ~1.2 s suspended inside
   the measured window but the max sample was only 4.0 ms,
   while the 0.13.1 test (8.4 s gap) showed the expected 10.4 s
   max sample. We think minstant's TSC may halt across some
   suspends and count through others. Repeat the test comparing
   detected gap vs max sample; if the TSC halts, per-sample
   timing silently loses suspend time — document either way.
6. CLAUDE.md governance model (design cogitation) [20]
7. Revisit probe adjustment under the in-interval vs
   call-to-call split: probes take one call per sample
   (inner=1), so the in-interval timer slice is unamortized
   and unmeasurable — an `adjusted` column can subtract
   nothing defensible; maybe state a bound instead
   [analysis](notes/design.md#timer-overhead-in-interval-vs-call-to-call)
8. Convert `harness` / `Bench` to probe-based measurement. Will
   likely need inner-loop support on `Probe` (batch N calls per
   sample; report divides by N and accounts for per-sample
   framing) so very-small workloads can still amortize timer
   overhead the way `run_adaptive` does today.
9. Rename app
10. Design an app to measure IIAC perforanace written in Rust[1]
11. `ice-ps-2t-wait` — iceoryx2 pub/sub with blocking waits via
    `Listener`/`Notifier` events; completes the {transport} ×
    {wait policy} matrix cell that compares against `mpsc-2t`
12. Switch ice benches to the loan-based zero-copy send path
    (`loan_uninit` + `send`) — the API a perf-sensitive user would
    use, and closer to iceoryx2's own benchmark method
13. Payload-size sweep for the round-trip benches (8 B / 8 KiB /
    1 MiB) — makes iceoryx2's size-independent latency vs channel
    copy cost visible in our own tables
14. `crossbeam-1t` / `crossbeam-2t` — `crossbeam-channel` directly
    (compare to mpsc-1t/2t which use crossbeam under the std API)
15. `tokio-mpsc-1t` / `tokio-mpsc-2t` — `tokio::sync::mpsc` round-trip
    inside a Tokio runtime (async overhead)
16. `flume-1t` / `flume-2t` — `flume` MPMC channel
17. Function-call baselines: direct call vs `Box<dyn Trait>` vs
    `async fn` (poll-once) — anchors the channel/serde numbers
    against the cheapest possible "send a value then receive it" path
18. When the second channel impl lands, extract shared message types
    + round-trip helpers into `src/benches/common.rs` (deferred from 0.2.0)
19. Additional thread control (count, per-thread pin lists, NUMA) —
    shape once a concrete bench needs it
20. Rename crate `iiac-perf` → general-purpose name (breaking; deferred)

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.
  iceoryx2 0.9.2 → 0.9.3) legitimately moves that bench's
  numbers and shouldn't ride in silently. Options considered
  (2026-07-08):
  - Caveat first: a Cargo **workspace shares one Cargo.lock**
    across members — it scopes deps per package (ice benches
    alone pay for iceoryx2; faster `-p` builds; harness/probes
    become a library crate) but does *not* give per-bench lock
    isolation, and it splits the single CLI into many binaries.
  - Targeted updates (`cargo update -p <crate>`, never bare
    `cargo update`) — ~90% of the provenance benefit at zero
    structure cost; adoptable immediately as discipline.
  - Feature gates (`--features ice`) — solves build weight in
    the current single package, not lock isolation.
  - Truly standalone crates (own Cargo.lock each) — the only
    real per-bench dep isolation; maximum maintenance, and cuts
    against "same harness, same build" A/B comparability.
  - Current lean: targeted-update discipline now; feature gates
    or workspace only when bench families multiply.
- clap CompleteEnv dynamic completion (the `unstable-dynamic`
  feature): clap's native runtime completer (`COMPLETE=bash
  iiac-perf`) would give bash die-hards a compact column view
  without carapace; revisit if clap stabilizes it.
